nameStory: Field dodder gets its name from its preference for open fields and agricultural areas, where it can find plenty of host plants to parasitize. The word 'dodder' comes from an old German word meaning 'to shake' or 'tremble,' referring to how these thread-like vines seem to quiver in the breeze as they search for their next victim.
description: Field dodder is a parasitic plant that looks nothing like what most people expect from a 'plant' – it's a tangle of thin, golden-yellow threads that wrap around other plants like living spaghetti. These orange to yellow stringy vines have no leaves and no roots once mature, surviving entirely by sucking nutrients from their host plants through specialized feeding structures. The threadlike stems can spread several feet, creating dense mats that can smother entire patches of vegetation.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Thin, thread-like orange to golden-yellow stems that twist and coil around host plants, forming tangled masses that look like orange yarn draped over vegetation

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Completely leafless – what might look like tiny leaves are actually just small scales pressed against the stem that you can barely feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Clusters of tiny white or cream-colored bell-shaped flowers, each smaller than a pencil eraser, that feel papery when touched and appear along the twining stems

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round seeds contained in papery capsules that split open when ripe, releasing seeds that are surprisingly large for such thin stems

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Stems feel smooth and slightly succulent, like thin cooked spaghetti, and will break cleanly when pulled rather than tearing like string

habitat: Field dodder thrives in open, sunny areas like agricultural fields, meadows, roadsides, and disturbed soils throughout New England. It particularly loves areas where legumes like clover and alfalfa grow, as these make excellent host plants. You'll often find it in farm fields, old pastures, and along field edges where it can spread from plant to plant.

seasonality.spring: Young dodder plants emerge from seed with tiny roots and a short green stem, but quickly lose their green color as they find host plants to parasitize.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the golden thread-like stems are most visible, spreading rapidly and producing small clusters of white flowers from July through September.
seasonality.fall: Stems turn more orange-brown and begin to die back after producing seeds, though the tangled masses remain visible draped over dead vegetation.
seasonality.winter: Completely dies back to the ground, surviving only as seeds that will germinate the following spring when soil warms up.

funFact: Field dodder is like a botanical vampire – it starts life as a normal plant with roots, but once it finds a host plant to parasitize, it actually kills off its own roots and becomes completely dependent on stealing nutrients from other plants, making it one of nature's most committed freeloaders!
confusionNotes: Field dodder is most easily confused with Five Angled Dodder, but field dodder has larger seeds and denser flower clusters. If you can find the flowers, field dodder's blooms are more crowded together, while five angled dodder has more scattered, individual flowers along the stems.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'weed,' field dodder is actually a native North American plant that has simply become very successful at spreading to new areas. Farmers consider it a serious pest because it can severely weaken or kill crop plants, and it's nearly impossible to remove without destroying the host plants it's wrapped around.
compareHints: Compared to other dodders in New England, field dodder produces the largest seeds and tends to form denser, more tangled masses. Scaldweed dodder is more commonly found in wetland edges, while field dodder prefers drier, open agricultural areas. Field dodder also has more compact flower clusters than most of its relatives, making the blooming stems look more 'bumpy' with flowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Scaldweed differs from its dodder relatives primarily in where it grows - it prefers wetter habitats than Field Dodder, and its stems tend to be slightly thicker than Five Angled Dodder.

Buttonbush Dodder differs from other New England dodders primarily by its wetland habitat and host preferences - while Field Dodder attacks crops and Scaldweed Dodder prefers woodland edges, Buttonbush Dodder is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Lizard's tail dodder is distinguished from other New England dodders primarily by its wetland habitat and highly specific host preference for lizard's tail plants.
Sessile Dodder is unique among New England dodders for specializing on woody hosts rather than soft-stemmed plants.
Smartweed Dodder is distinguished from other New England dodders primarily by its habitat and host preferences - it's the wetland specialist of the dodder family.
Among New England's dodder species, hazel dodder is distinguished by its preference for woody shrubs rather than herbaceous plants.
Five Angled Dodder is much rarer in New England than the common Scaldweed dodder, and prefers wetter habitats compared to Field Dodder's preference for dry agricultural areas.
